title: If I Forgive Them, Do I Have to Trust Them Again?
excerpt: Forgiveness, trust and reconciliation are three different things, and much of the pain people carry comes from being told they are one. Jesus asks the first of every disciple. The second is earned, and the third takes two.
body:
A woman's father has started coming to church again after twenty years of drinking, and he wants to see his grandchildren. She remembers what the house was like when she was nine. A man found out about his wife's affair last spring, and his small group keeps asking whether he has forgiven her yet, in a tone that suggests the right answer would also settle whether he has moved back in. A young pastor was let go after he raised questions about the senior pastor's temper, and the elders have asked him to meet that man for coffee and put it all behind them. A grandmother has forgiven her son-in-law for what he did to her daughter, and has been told by a relative that if she had really forgiven him she would have him over for Thanksgiving.

Each of them was asked whether they had forgiven. What they were really being asked was whether they would let the person back in.

The skeptic has watched this for a long time and has a hard thing to say. Christianity, he says, asks the injured to forgive and asks very little of the people who injured them. It tells a battered wife that love "bears all things" (1 Corinthians 13:7) and tells a congregation to protect a pastor's ministry. It calls this grace. To him it looks like a system for making victims carry the cost of other people's sins, and he has seen enough of it to think the system is working as designed.

He has seen something real, and the church should say so before it says anything else. But the teaching he has met is not the teaching of the Bible. It has run three different things together, and pulling them apart is most of the work this essay has to do.

Some readers come to this question with an injury that is still open, and the argument below can wait for them. The site's page for the person who [can't forgive](/help/cant-forgive) says the most important thing in a single sentence: "You can forgive someone and still report them, keep your distance, or refuse contact." It also says this: "If the person who hurt you is still a danger to you or to a child, safety comes first." If that is you, start there, and [Find Help](/help) has the hotlines. If the wound came from a church, the page for the person the [church hurt](/help/church-hurt) was written for you. Nothing in this essay is legal advice.

## Three Words We Have Run Together

Forgiveness, trust and reconciliation are related, and they are not the same thing. Most of the damage done in this area comes from treating them as one.

Forgiveness is about a debt. When someone wrongs you, something is owed: an apology, a repayment, a reckoning. To forgive is to give up your claim to collect it yourself. You stop trying to make them pay, in the courtroom you keep in your head at three in the morning and in the small revenges that wounded people learn to take. You hand the case to God. Paul put it this way to Christians who had real enemies: "Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, 'Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord'" (Romans 12:19). Forgiveness does not say the debt was small. It says the debt is real, and that you are no longer the one who will collect it.

Trust is something else. It is a judgment about the future, a confidence that a person will act a certain way, and it rests on evidence. You can forgive a man completely and still have no evidence at all that he will not do it again. Trust is not owed. It is earned, usually slowly, sometimes never. A woman who forgives the babysitter who neglected her child is not obliged to hire her back. That is not a failure of forgiveness. It is ordinary wisdom, the kind Jesus asked of his disciples when he sent them out "wise as serpents and innocent as doves" (Matthew 10:16).

Reconciliation is a third thing. It is the restoring of a relationship, and a relationship has two people in it. You can forgive someone who is dead, or who never apologized, or who doesn't know you exist. You can't be reconciled to them. Reconciliation needs the one who did the harm to own it, to turn, and to be changed by turning. Paul knew how much of this lay outside a person's control: "If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all" (Romans 12:18). Two qualifications sit in that one sentence. Peace may not be possible, and only one side of it depends on you.

When these three are run together, forgiveness becomes a trap. If forgiving means trusting, then the woman cannot forgive her father without handing him her children. If forgiving means reconciling, then the man cannot forgive his wife without pretending the marriage is what it was. So the person who was hurt is left with two choices, both bad: refuse to forgive and be told they are bitter, or forgive and be told to walk back into the room where they were hurt. The page on forgiveness names the problem exactly: "Much of the pressure you feel comes from people who have mashed those three together."

## What Jesus Said, and What He Asked

None of this softens what Jesus said about forgiveness, and an honest essay has to let him say it at full strength. When Peter asked how often he had to forgive a brother, and offered seven times as a generous answer, Jesus said, "I do not say to you seven times, but seventy-seven times" (Matthew 18:22). Then he told of a servant forgiven a debt no one could ever repay, who went out and seized a fellow servant by the throat over a small one. The parable ends with words that should make any of us careful: "So also my heavenly Father will do to every one of you, if you do not forgive your brother from your heart" (Matthew 18:35).

We are capable of calling a grudge a boundary, and of keeping a person at a distance for years in the name of wisdom when it is really the pleasure of keeping them in debt. The servant in the parable did not think of himself as cruel. He thought he was owed.

But Luke records the same teaching with a detail Matthew leaves out. "Pay attention to yourselves! If your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him, and if he sins against you seven times in the day, and turns to you seven times, saying, 'I repent,' you must forgive him" (Luke 17:3-4). There is a rebuke in that sentence, and there is repentance. Jesus does not tell the injured person to keep quiet. He tells them to name the wrong, and he describes forgiveness as something that answers a turning.

Faithful Christians read these two passages in two ways, and both readings are held by serious people. Some say that the forgiveness of the heart is owed always, whether the other person repents or not, because the servant in Matthew was not asked to wait for an apology; the giving up of revenge cannot depend on the other person's choices. Others say that forgiveness in its full sense, the kind that restores the relationship, waits for repentance, as Luke describes and as God's own forgiveness waits on our turning to him; what is owed before that is the refusal of revenge and a readiness to forgive. The page on forgiveness puts the common ground in one sentence: "Both agree on what you can do tonight, which is to give up revenge and hand the case to God, and both say reconciliation waits for real repentance."

That common ground is enough to answer the question in the title. Forgiving someone does not require you to trust them again. Neither reading of Jesus asks it.

## What Joseph Did Before He Wept

Genesis tells the longest story of forgiveness in the Old Testament, and it is worth noticing how slowly it moves. Joseph's brothers sold him into slavery when he was seventeen. More than twenty years later they came to Egypt to buy grain and bowed before a governor they did not recognize. He knew them at once. He did not tell them who he was.

What he did instead has puzzled readers for a long time. He accused them of being spies. He kept one of them in prison. He sent them home and demanded that they come back with the youngest brother, Benjamin, the other son of Joseph's mother, and then he arranged things so that Benjamin appeared to be a thief who would have to stay behind as a slave. Some readers have found this cruel. It is better read as a test, and the question it put to the brothers was the one that mattered: had they changed? Twenty years earlier they had sold one of Rachel's sons and gone home with a lie. Would they now abandon the other one to save themselves?

The brothers' first answer came before they knew he understood their language. "In truth we are guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the distress of his soul, when he begged us and we did not listen" (Genesis 42:21). The Study Bible's note on [Genesis 42](/study/bible/genesis/42) observes that this is where "we learn for the first time that he pleaded with them," a detail the account of the sale left out. Joseph turned away and wept. He still did not reveal himself.

The second answer came when Judah, the brother who had proposed selling Joseph in the first place, offered himself as a slave in Benjamin's place so that the boy could go home to their father (Genesis 44:33). Only then did Joseph send everyone else out of the room, and only then did he say, "I am your brother, Joseph, whom you sold into Egypt" (Genesis 45:4). He did not say that what they had done was nothing. He named it in the same sentence. And then he said, "do not be distressed or angry with yourselves because you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life" (Genesis 45:5). The note on [Genesis 45](/study/bible/genesis/45) observes that "His first question is about his father, and his first explanation is about God."

Joseph's heart seems to have been moving toward his brothers long before that day; he wept at the first sight of their guilt. But he did not hand them his trust until he had seen what kind of men they had become. Years later, when their father died and they feared he had only been waiting, he answered them with words Christians have leaned on ever since: "As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today" (Genesis 50:20).

The New Testament has a smaller story with the same shape. When Saul of Tarsus came to Jerusalem after his conversion, the disciples there "were all afraid of him, for they did not believe that he was a disciple" (Acts 9:26). They had good reason. He had dragged their friends to prison. Luke does not scold them for their fear. Barnabas took Saul to the apostles and told them what had happened to him, and the church came to trust him through a witness and over time. Repentance was real in Saul's case, and trust still had to be built.

## The Fear on Each Side

Two people can read everything above and come away afraid, and both of their fears deserve to be stated properly.

The first is the person who has been hurt, and who has heard forgiveness preached as a weapon. They fear that if they say the word, their family will take "I forgive him" to mean "he can come to Christmas," and their church will take it to mean the matter is closed. This fear is not bitterness. It is what experience has taught them, and the experience is often accurate. For them the distinctions above are what make it possible to obey Jesus without walking back into danger.

The second is the Christian who has watched the word "boundary" do a great deal of work in recent years and wonders whether it has become a respectable name for unforgiveness. They know families that stopped speaking over offenses that could have been borne, and people who learned the language of self-protection and used it to keep every relationship on their own terms. They are not wrong either. A heart that has been wronged can turn its wound into a fortress and live there for the rest of its life.

The answer to both is the same distinction, used honestly. Forgiveness concerns your heart toward the debt, and that you owe, however slowly it comes. Trust concerns your judgment about the future, and that you don't owe; it follows evidence. Reconciliation concerns the relationship, and it waits on the other person's repentance. A boundary that protects you or a child from real harm is not unforgiveness. A boundary kept up long after the person has truly changed, kept because it is satisfying to keep them out, may be. Only you and God can tell which one you are holding, and it is worth asking him.

## Where We Have Failed

The skeptic's charge is not only about bad theology. It is about what churches have done with it, and here I have to speak as one of the people responsible. I'm a pastor. The page on forgiveness says what many of us have done, and it says it better than I would: "Churches and families have often wanted forgiveness mainly because it's quieter. It keeps the holidays calm, a respected man's name clean, and a ministry out of the news, and it lets everyone move on except the person who was hurt."

We have asked the wounded to forgive quickly and asked the guilty for almost nothing. We have hurried people to reconciliation because an unresolved conflict was bad for the church. We have treated a victim's anger as the problem to be solved and the abuser's reputation as the asset to be protected. Jeremiah described prophets who did this to Israel: "They have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying, 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace" (Jeremiah 6:14). A wound healed lightly does not heal. It closes over the infection.

Friedrich Nietzsche argued in *On the Genealogy of Morality* (1887) that Christian forgiveness was weakness in disguise, the revenge of people too powerless to take any other kind. Where the church has asked the weak to forgive so that the strong can stay comfortable, it has given him his evidence. But the forgiveness Scripture describes is not the surrender of the powerless. It is a decision to give up revenge because there is a Judge who will not let the wrong go unanswered. That is why it can sit beside a police report.

## When It Was Abuse

Some of what people are asked to forgive is not an ordinary sin between equals. It is abuse: violence in a home, the sexual abuse of a child, the long control of one person by another, the misuse of spiritual authority to silence and harm. Here the distinctions above become matters of safety, and the church's duty becomes plain.

No one should ever be told that forgiveness requires them to return to a person who is hurting them. Paul's own sentence, "so far as it depends on you," admits that peace with some people is not possible. Forgiveness does not cancel the consequences of a crime, and reporting a crime is not revenge; Paul called the governing authority God's servant to punish wrongdoing in the very next chapter of the same letter (Romans 13:4). A woman can forgive the man who abused her and testify against him. A congregation can forgive a leader and still remove him, report him, and never let him near children again. These are not failures of grace. They are what love does when it takes harm seriously.

Churches have duties here that are not optional. The page for those [hurt by the church](/help/church-hurt) tells leaders: "Never ask a victim to meet their abuser to reconcile, never ask them to keep quiet, and never make them tell their story again and again to a room of leaders." Many states require clergy to report suspected child abuse, and the rules differ from place to place; a pastor who does not know the law where he serves should learn it before he needs it. Where a child may be at risk, the matter goes to the authorities, not to a meeting of elders. If you are reading this as a church leader, this paragraph is the most important one in the essay.

## If You Are Carrying This Now

If you are the one who was hurt, you don't have to settle all of this tonight, and some of it you shouldn't try to settle alone. If you are not safe, safety is the only question this week. If you are safe, the forgiveness page suggests a simple exercise: write three words across a page, forgive, trust and contact, and decide them separately. You may find that you are ready to begin the first long before the second, and that the third is not yours to decide until the other person has changed.

Begin forgiveness with honesty. Tell God exactly what was done and what it cost; the psalms give you language for it. You can't release a debt you won't count, and God is not asking you to pretend the debt was small. He is asking you to let him hold it.

If you are the one who did the harm, the way back is not through asking for trust. It is through owning what you did without excuses, accepting the consequences, making what amends you can, and letting time and changed behavior speak. Zacchaeus did not ask Jesus to tell everyone he was trustworthy now. He paid people back (Luke 19:8). Trust that is demanded is not trust. It has to be given, and you can only make it possible.

If you are a friend or a church member, stop asking the wounded person whether they have forgiven yet. Ask whether they are safe, and whether there is anything you can carry for them.

## The One Who Did Not Threaten

Peter, who once asked Jesus how often he had to forgive, later wrote about what Jesus did when he was wronged. "When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly" (1 Peter 2:23). That is forgiveness in its plainest form: the refusal of revenge, and the handing of the case to a Judge.

Notice what Jesus did not do. He did not say that what was done to him was nothing. He did not tell the people who crucified him that they were safe to keep doing it. He prayed, "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do" (Luke 23:34), and he left judgment where it belonged. Three days later he came back, and the first people he went to find were the friends who had abandoned him. He made breakfast for one of them on a beach and asked him three times whether he loved him (John 21:15-17). Forgiveness had already been given. The relationship was restored one honest question at a time.

The woman whose father wants to see his grandchildren may be able to forgive him long before she can trust him, and she does not sin by waiting to see what kind of man he has become. The man whose wife betrayed him may forgive her and still not know yet what their marriage will be. The young pastor may forgive the man who forced him out without pretending, over coffee, that nothing happened. They have been asked to do something hard. They have not been asked to do something foolish. And the One who asks it of them has not asked anything he did not do himself, at a cost none of us will ever be asked to pay.

*"Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God."* (Romans 12:19)

*"Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you."* (Ephesians 4:32)
